titles.topic: Chemical Equilibria: Reversible Reactions & Dynamic Equilibrium

blocks.md:
- Some reactions go to completion where the reactants are used up to form the products and the reaction stops when all the reactants are used up
- In **reversible reactions,** the products can react to reform the original reactants
- To show a reversible reaction, two opposing half arrows are used: ⇌

blocks.alt: Forward reaction: hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO4.5H2O(s), forms anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water. Reverse reaction: anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water form the hydrated salt. The two are combined into one equation with an equilibrium arrow.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows an example of a forward and reverse reaction that can be written as one equation using two half arrows

blocks.md:
- In a **dynamic equilibrium,** the forward and reverse reactions both continue to take place, at the same rate
- In a dynamic equilibrium:

  - The **rate** of the **forward** reaction is the same as the rate of the **reverse** reaction in a **closed system**
  - The **concentrations **of the **reactants **and **products **are **constant**

blocks.alt: Particle diagram of a closed container holding a mixture of hydrogen molecules, iodine molecules and hydrogen iodide molecules, with a key for hydrogen and iodine atoms.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows a snapshot of a dynamic equilibrium in which molecules of hydrogen iodide are breaking down to hydrogen and iodine at the same rate as hydrogen and iodine molecules are reacting together to form hydrogen iodide

blocks.text: Diagrams showing reactant and product concentration as a reaction approaches equilibrium

blocks.alt: Graph showing product concentration increasing to 10 mol dm⁻³ and reactant concentration decreasing to 1 mol dm⁻³, reaching equilibrium over time.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows that the concentration of the reactants and products does not change anymore once equilibrium has been reached (equilibrium was approached using reactants)

blocks.alt: Graph showing concentration changes over time, reaching equilibrium. Red line decreases to 10 mol/dm³; green line increases to 1 mol/dm³.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows that the concentration of the reactants and products does not change anymore once equilibrium has been reached (equilibrium was approached using products)

blocks.md:
- A **closed system **is one in which none of the reactants or products escape from the reaction mixture
- In an **open system**, matter and energy can be lost to the surroundings
- When a reaction takes place entirely in solution, equilibrium can be reached in open flasks as a negligible amount of material is lost through evaporation
- If the reaction involves gases, equilibrium can only be reached in a closed system

blocks.text: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate in a closed system

blocks.alt: Diagram illustrating the equilibrium reaction of calcium carbonate decomposing into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide, with a particle key below.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows a closed system in which no carbon dioxide gas can escape and the calcium carbonate is in equilibrium with the calcium oxide and carbon dioxide

blocks.text: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate in an open system

blocks.alt: A diagram shows the thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate (CaCO3) into calcium oxide (CaO) and carbon dioxide gas (CO2) in a container.
blocks.caption: The diagram shows an open system in which the calcium carbonate is continually decomposing as the carbon dioxide is lost causing the reaction to eventually go to completion

blocks.label: Exam Hint
blocks.md:
A common misconception is to think that the concentrations of the reactants and products are **equal.**

However, they are** not equal**, but they **remain constant** at dynamic equilibrium (i.e. the concentrations are not changing).

The concentrations will change as the reaction progresses, only **until the equilibrium** is reached.
